catalog_quote: § 10. Betonung. a. Der Wortakzent wird weitgehend durch den Satzrhythmus und den mit dem Satzteil verbundenen Affekt bestimmt: fikfál 47—fíhrub 37, ilá ḍlamat 73—ila ghábat 81, grúbū 848—úgrubū 863. (Weiteres in § 11). b. Doch darf als Hauptregel für den Wortakzent festgelegt werden, dass dieser das Bestreben hat, sich soweit als möglich vom Ende des Wortes, bezw. der Betonungseinheit zurückzuziehen. Dies bringt das Jemenische vielfach der traditionellen Betonung des Schriftarabischen nahe, unterscheidet es aber davon aufs deutlichste, indem geschlossene oder lange Silben keineswegs immer ein Hindernis für die Zurücknahme des Tones bilden: ǧáu̯āb 75, hídār 110 (aber natürlich auch hidâr 136), ǧíhīm 200, ar-rábūʿ „Mittwoch“, máǧnūn 100, míḥibb 1425, ʿîdān 762, gáʿādäh 143, ʿádaltū 167. Daher bágdanūs (äg., pal. baqdûnis) „Petersilie“, dâzinäh (auch târzīnäh, äg., pal. dazzîna) „Dutzend“,…

new_statements.translation: § 10. Stress. a. Word accent is largely determined by sentence rhythm and by the affect attached to the phrase [...]. b. Yet as the main rule for word accent it may be laid down that it strives to withdraw as far as possible from the end of the word, or rather of the stress unit. This often brings Yemeni close to the traditional accentuation of Written Arabic, but distinguishes it from it most clearly in that closed or long syllables are by no means always an obstacle to the retraction of the accent: ǧáu̯ab, hídar, ǧíhīm, ar-rábūʿ 'Wednesday', máǧnūn, míḥibb, ʿídān, gáʿadäh, ʿádaltū.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main rule: stress retracts as far as possible toward the beginning of the word (stress unit), i.e. to the first syllable, and heavy (closed or long) syllables do not reliably block the retraction (máǧnūn, míḥibb, ʿídān, gáʿadäh, ʿádaltū, bágdanūs 'parsley', dâzināh 'dozen'); this is only a tendency, since sentence rhythm and emphasis shift the accent freely (fikfál ~ fíhrub; grúbū ~ úgrubū), and semantically subordinate words (article, prepositions, negations, conjunctions, vocative particle) often attract the stress (§10 c). §11 adds that short-vowel elision, not a primary accent shift, creates the variable stressings of grammatically identical forms. Modern description (Shachmon 2022, via Klimiuk 2023) likewise stresses the instability of Yemeni stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is pulled by sentence rhythm and affect (§10 a); doublets like hídar / hidâr; subordinate function words often carry the accent in the phrase (§10 c); word-initial consonant clusters with a strongly stressed final vowel (§11 b: 'Hierbei wird der Endvokal stark betont'); Goitein marks deviations from rule b in his transcriptions (§10 d).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is explicitly the 'Betonungseinheit' (stress unit) rather than the isolated word; the data are proverbs and sayings elicited from recent immigrants from central Yemen in Jerusalem, so no citation-form study. Variety: the urban Jewish dialect of Ṣanʿāʾ and ʿAmrān (p. xii). The book is a proverb collection whose 'Zur Sprache' introduction (pp. xii–xxiv) is a phonology/morphology sketch.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Goitein 1934) describes the urban Jewish dialect of central Yemen, essentially Ṣanʿāʾ and ʿAmrān (p. xii: 'Die hier vorgelegte Sprache ist die der städtischen Juden Zentral-jemens, im wesentlichen derjenigen von San‘a und ‘Amran'), recorded from recent immigrants in Jerusalem around 1928–1934. That is the central variety of jude1267 / ISO jye (no separate glottocode). Goitein 1960 covers the Lower-Yemen Jewish village dialect of al-Gades; Shachmon 2022 covers the whole Jewish Yemeni spectrum and reports considerable instability of stress across varieties. Note that the Muslim Ṣanʿāʾ dialect (sana1295) has a separate literature (Rossi 1939, Watson 1993/2002) not used here.
